utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't understand. The HVO was proclaimed enemy, but by whom? You didn't say it, or I didn't get it in the interpretation anyway.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the information was conveyed to me that the media had announced, the media under the supervision of the BH army and the Bosniak Muslims, that is to say, via the media, that the HVO was proclaimed an enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please go on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I received information that policemen Vlado Lesic, Zeljko Barbic, and Zvonko Bilic were the perpetrators of the incident with the soldier at the Ovnak checkpoint and I asked that they be distanced from the checkpoint and that they should not carry on with their duties there and that disciplinary measures be taken against them and that the commander of the police should inform me about the disciplinary measures that had been taken. I was not able to contact the commander but I had this talk with the officer on duty at the military police station because I was not able to come into contact with him. They couldn't tell me where the chief of police was at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "The commander of the police." Interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: On that day I also received information about the incidents in the town of Travnik where again there were mutual arrests carried out and other forms of violating the public law and order. I again requested that UNPROFOR visit the Travnik municipality territory, that is, Grahovcici and Brajkovici, because I had received information that this area was completely surrounded and isolated without any communication and was surrounded by the BH army forces. At 14.00 on the 14th of May, I also received information that all Gypsies from the Vitez municipality area were preparing to leave, to move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell us what religion the Gypsies were in the area?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I believe that they were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: There were over 500, and their intention was to go to Novi Travnik and Travnik escorted by UNPROFOR. I expressed my disagreement with this decision to leave the Vitez area, and I called the mayor of Vitez and asked him for assistance in mediating in order that we would prevent the Gypsies from leaving. I asked that the mayor, Ivica Santic, talk to the representatives of the Gypsies and their leaders and to let them know that we would do all we can so that they could stay in their homes where they had lived until then. I had a problem with the communications officer who had come to me. He was the UNPROFOR officer. I think his name was Perry. I don't know whether this was his name or nickname. He was the liaison officer there. He said that I was not allowing this group of about 500 Gypsies to leave. I told him that in these circumstances, such freedom of movement would amount to moving of the Gypsies out of the Lasva Valley and that in that sense, it was contrary to the position of the UNHCR, who was not allowing such transfers of people. I also told him that the mayor was conducting discussions with the representatives of their own, and if despite all our efforts the decision by the leadership of Gypsies was such that they would still leave, we would let them go. However, we were lucky in our efforts, and we managed to keep this group of Gypsies in the area, and, to date, they continue to live in the territory of Vitez municipality. In the course of the day, another 50 families arrived. They came from Zenica. They had been kept at the checkpoint Lasva, which was controlled by the BH army, the main Zenica-Busovaca road, and they had waited here to be permitted to get a permit from the BH army in order to be able to move to Vitez and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were these Croatian families from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were Croatian families from Zenica region, and they were arriving daily. Every day there was a certain number of families who arrived there. On 15 May, 1993, I received information from the intelligence service that the BH army was conducting regrouping and that during the following day combat operations could be expected. I visited the lines of Vitez that day, and in the course of the day I attempted to again contact the commander of the military police. However, again I was unable to reach him. I also issued an order to the Frankopan Brigade commander, asking him to take control of the checkpoint at Ovnak where that incident had occurred, but the brigade commander was unable to implement this order. He informed me that he received a reply from the policemen who were on duty, telling him that he had no authority over them and that they were receiving orders from their own commander. I also received information that the BH army was bringing in new forces to Vitez and Busovaca. Also, reinforcements were observed coming from Bugojno to the area of Novi Travnik on the same day. After this information reached me about deployment of new forces and taking into account that Zupa Gora and Brajkovici, had now been surrounded, I asked for a meeting with Colonel Duncan, and at 16.30 I had a meeting. I asked of him to mediate in order that the agreement between the BH army and the HVO be implemented, and I informed him on all the information I had gathered until that point about the regroupings and bringing in of fresh forces and preparations for attack, knowing that the UNPROFOR bases -- with a mind that the UNPROFOR base was also in that same area. I advised Colonel Duncan that -- he said that we were in a very difficult situation, and I responded that we had to defend ourselves because we had no other solution. After that meeting, on the same day I also received information about movement of 11 bus loads of soldiers, that is, of the BH army from the direction of Zenica towards Vitez. Through Nakic, a member of the joint command, I asked to mediate in organising a meeting with the representatives of the 3rd Corps, with the commander Enver Hadzihasanovic, that is, so that we would prevent this attack which was being prepared. I also received information from the Military Intelligence Service that new and fresh forces were also being brought in to Fojnica via Mount Igman and Tarcin. I also received information about the arrest of civilians in Novi Travnik by members of the 308th BH Army Brigade and these arrested civilians were Croat. On the 17th of May, 1993, we had an incident at the headquarters in Vitez and in a family home -- or the apartment where Dominik Sakic, who had been expelled from Zenica, was temporarily taking his quarters. A military policeman had forcibly entered his apartment, physically abused him, and robbed him in the presence of his own family, after which they came to the Hotel Vitez and beat up Zivko Totic, who several days earlier had been released by the 7th Muslim Brigade. Zivko Totic was the HVO commander in Zenica, by the way. I again asked for an investigation by the military police regarding these incidents but I still had not received any reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, these incidents were taking place at the Ovnak checkpoint, in the Hotel Vitez, in Dominik Sakic's private apartment and each time you ask for an investigation. This is a usual thing or should the military police have, by its official duties, launched such an investigation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, its official duty would have been and this is part of their job description. The military police was supposed to launch an investigation and identify the perpetrators. Unfortunately, they themselves took part in these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, to your understanding of your own position, in military terms, that is, as commander of the Operative Zone, is it your duty to pursue and take care of each individual incident or is your duty to ensure that the system worked?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Of course, my duty is to organise the system in such a way that it works, and I would not be able to pursue every single individual incident, and I would not be able to function as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So how could you describe a situation in which you are forced, as if you were just a simple police officer, to point to every single incident that was perpetrated either by them or by somebody else and they do not pursue or investigate?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: These were very -- we were in conditions where we had a very complex situation. Also, it was part of my effort to push through the changes within the chain of command and authorities over the military police, with my own superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, all these problems that you have just mentioned regarding the military police at that time, did you transmit the information to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: My superiors received both the regular reports and extraordinary reports. For instance, the incident which was the assault on Commander Totic, who had just been released, I would especially send such reports, as I did in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was your goal regarding each of the incidents regarding the military police? You showered, practically, your superiors in Mostar with those?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I was looking to get a reaction and trigger off changes because I received information from my assistant for information that there were a number of individuals within the military police who had criminal records. So I wanted changes in the structure and composition of the military police, as well as in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Please move on. How did events unfold after that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 13.55, I was informed by mayor Santic that the persecution of Muslims were continuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you going to use documents, written reports relating to the chain of command? The accused is saying that he proposed some changes. Are there any reports where all the events he's talking about are referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we had the witness (redacted) (redacted), and he testified to that. However, unfortunately, the Defence was unable to obtain documents from the military police archives and the Defence did not manage to receive any information from the main staff archives. So those two sources have remained inaccessible to the Defence, so that the Defence has had no access to any of the documents which General Blaskic sent to his superiors in Mostar. But as witness (redacted) testified, changes were affected, and later on General Blaskic will testify as to the changes, the real changes, which happened with respect to the military police and the special purpose units, especially with the Vitezovi special units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Very well. At 13.55, I had a conversation with mayor Santic, who again informed me and discussed the problem that despite all the measures taken the Bosniak Muslims were still leaving the town. He said that members of the military police and members of the Vitezovi special purpose units were at the forefront of such activities and that they were even engaging in selling of apartments that they had taken. I called both of the commanders of these units and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please name them?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Darko Kraljevic and Mr. Pasko Ljubicic. I asked that orders be issued to their immediate subordinates in the spirit of my own order against the expulsion and that copies of such orders be sent to my attention. However, unfortunately, I never managed to receive copies of such documents. I then called Santic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who is Santic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Santic was the mayor of Vitez. I asked him to engage the civilian police in preventing the expulsions of Muslims, and if it turns out that they were unable to prevent these expulsions, to at least register the incidents so that we had some kind of control over the situation. At 17.10 on the 17th of May, I had a meeting with the liaison officer of the British Battalion, and I again asked him to inform Colonel Duncan and mediate in organising a meeting between myself and the commander of the 3rd Corps of the BH army. The Military Intelligence Service also informed me that Radio Sarajevo was broadcasting information that there were mass graves of Muslims in Vitez and that it could create a certain atmosphere leading to another attack by the BH army. Again, the movements of the BH army had been observed in the Lasva operative group zone. On the 18th of May, 1993, I held a press conference in Busovaca, around 11.00, and, in this press conference, I publicly spoke about the problems of the persecution of Bosniak Muslims, and I asked that the military police issue an order which would prevent expulsions of Bosnian Muslims from their residences. I still had not received copies of these orders as I had asked. I also asked to be fully informed by the security service regarding these incidents of forcible expulsions and again I never received it. On the 18th of May, 1993, about 79 new families arrived in Vitez and Busovaca from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were these Croatian families?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were Croatian families which had been expelled from Zenica, and they arrived in Busovaca and Vitez. I also received information that disciplinary measures had been taken regarding these expulsions of Bosniak Muslims. There were two policemen, Pranjkovic and Tomic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We don't have the names there, so please repeat the whole sentence.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I received information --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If you can just slow down a little bit? So what was the information about?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Information that disciplinary measures had been taken against the soldiers who had carried out expulsions of the Bosniak Muslims from their apartments, and their names were Zeljko Pranjkovic and Zdravko Tomic. At 17.00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What kind of sanctions were they? You are saying that disciplinary measures were taken, at least you were informed about it, but what kind of measures were they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I only have a note "disciplinary measures," which probably meant military detention. I assume this, but I do not know how many days of detention because there was a separate log where all the disciplinary measures were recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We can perhaps take a break here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Shall we take a break now? Are you done with the day the 18th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Exactly. We have just finished with the day, and this would be a good point to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, I think we have finished with the 18th of May, '93. Can we go on from there with the chronology of the most important events?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of May, 1993, the town of Vitez was shelled by artillery from Kruscica and Sivrino Selo, areas controlled by the BH army. I again issued an order on the 19th of May, 1993, that the International Red Cross officers be enabled to carry out their mandate regardless of whether those visits had been announced previously or not. I was informed by the assistant for information in the course of the day, the day being the 19th of May, that the soldiers on the front line were fatigued, exhausted, morale was low, they were hungry, and generally morale was rather low. I was also informed that eleven soldiers had been taken into custody, former members of the HVO brigade in Zenica who had engaged in the persecution of Bosniak Muslims and evicted them from their homes in the municipality of Vitez. I was also informed that the BH army had shelled Guca Gora, an area under the control of the HVO in Travnik. At 10.00, I had a meeting with the liaison officer of the UN commander, Colonel Duncan, and I asked him to take steps so as to remove BH army snipers from the position of Grbavica as the area of Grbavica had to be demilitarised pursuant to the agreement of the 20th of April, 1993, an agreement signed by the two commanders, that is, of the HVO and of the BH army, Halilovic and Petkovic. The UNPROFOR liaison officer informed me that there were HVO snipers operating also in the vicinity of the UNPROFOR base, and after the meeting ended, I called up the commander of the Viteska Brigade, Cerkez, and checked him whether the sniper rifles had been confiscated, and Cerkez informed me that he had provided a list of all confiscated sniper rifles to the command and that the members of the Vitez Brigade had no sniper rifles left. I told the commander of the Vitez Brigade that, if necessary, he should lock up the sniper rifles in his office and keep them personally under lock and key in one of the cupboards in his office in the headquarters of the Vitez Brigade. Once again, the problem of food came up because refugees were arriving on a daily basis and our reserves were very low, virtually non-existent. On the 20th of May, 1993, I was informed by the Military Intelligence Service that about 2.000 soldiers of the BH army had left Sarajevo via Igman and Tarcin and that they would be deployed in the forthcoming operation and attack against the HVO. In this report of the Military Intelligence, I was told that the BH army would fight to the end, which meant until they captured the area controlled by the HVO. I was also informed by the Military Intelligence Service that, in the area of Slimena, which is a neighbourhood in the Travnik municipality, parts of the 17th Krajina Brigade had arrived, the brigade of the BH army, numbering 250 to 300 men, and that they had been accommodated in the family homes of the Bosniak Muslims in the Slimena neighbourhood. On the 21st of May, 1993, I was informed on a visit by the joint command in Kakanj and, in the course of the day, I was also informed that two officers of the HVO had been killed belonging to the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade and that this had been done when they were driving from Novi Travnik to the front line at Kamenjas-Mravinjac. They were killed in an ambush in an area controlled by the BH army. In Novi Travnik, Muslims were being exchanged for Croats in a part of the town controlled by the HVO or the BH army respectively at a certain price and commission. I asked that the people manning the checkpoints should be checked so that by selecting more reliable officers, the incidents and problems at the checkpoints would be eliminated. I was informed on casualties in the Lasva River Valley, and according to the information available to us at the time, that is, on the 21st of May, we had 124 dead soldiers, 10 missing, 13 captured, and 323 wounded soldiers. In the afternoon of the 21st of May, an armed conflict broke out in Nova Bila between members of the military police and members of the Vitezovi special purpose unit. I managed to get in touch with the commander of the Vitezovi special purpose unit, that is, Darko Kraljevic, and I asked that an end be put to incidents and the provocation of such incidents and that he should take measures against the members of his unit. From the assistant for security, I was informed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, General Blaskic. These incidents between members of the military police and the Vitezovi -- is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Between the military police of the HVO and the members of the Vitezovi in Nova Bila, that is what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Over what did those incidents occur? What was the cause?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember what the cause was of the incident, but I have note of it, that there was an armed conflict between these two groups. I cannot recollect; I could only guess as to the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. A further point of clarification: You covered very quickly that there was a visit on that same day by the joint commission. Was it a joint commission or the joint command? As the transcript goes very quickly, I'm not sure what you said. Was it the joint command? We're talking about the 21st of May.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The joint command was already operational at that time, and at lower levels, there were joint commissions, Mr. President. I said the joint command but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. A joint command that made a visit. A further point of clarification: What was the meaning of these visits? They would seem to be rather futile because fighting continued between you and the BH army. What was discussed at these visits? The front against Republika Srpska? What? It is rather strange for a commander like you not to say what they discussed, actually.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the joint command, ever since the 21st of April, '93, when it started working, it was still operational, and it continued working both at the level of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also at the level of the 3rd Corps and the Operative Zone. They had daily meetings and, according to a plan of their own, they toured areas which they felt they needed to visit or which perhaps I or the commander of the 3rd Corps requested, regardless of the fact that we hadn't achieved a cessation of hostilities in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But during this visit, did you participate at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I did not, but I asked, and I had asked for some time, that a meeting be held between me and the commander of the 3rd Corps. I had asked that through the liaison officer of UNPROFOR, through Colonel Duncan, and through this joint command. I had appealed that they organise a meeting between me and the 3rd Corps commander because, on the one hand, we had armed hostilities, the conflict was ongoing, and on the other side, we had joint commitments, and the joint command was working, planning joint activities towards Vlasic, the liberation of Vlasic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is precisely there that I find it difficult to understand what was said. Did they discuss what they were doing between themselves or their common enemy. I didn't make many notes. Suddenly there were 2.000 soldiers. For example, you said the day before you received information that 2.000 soldiers from the Bosnian army were coming from Sarajevo, and that you learnt that the Bosnian army would fight till the end. That is what you said?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Then the next day you attend a meeting of the joint command. What did you say then? You are fighting who? "Are you fighting against us or are you fighting Republika Srpska?" What was your role in that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was not present at the meeting of the joint command, but my deputy, Mr. Franjo Nakic, and the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, Mr. Dzemo Merdan. So they attended meetings every day. When I received this report, and not just this report, any information, when I received it regarding the regrouping of forces, I asked for a meeting with the commander of the 3rd Corps, but I didn't have the opportunity to tell him that. I would have probably told him about the regrouping and about the planned attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps, but perhaps not you, General Blaskic, but you were represented there, after all. It seems to me, but I'm not a commander at war, if I learnt that 2.000 soldiers were moving from Sarajevo not to fight Republika Srpska but to fight against me, it seems to me that I would have said, "What kind of war is this?" or I would have gone to that joint command meeting and said, "Who is waging war against whom and with whom?" That is what I don't understand. When you tell us this very detailed chronology, you pass over a point. For instance, you stay the 21st of May there was an visit by the joint command, two HVO officers are killed, 2.000 soldiers are coming and they're going to fight until the end. This is, after all, a bit difficult to follow. This is rather surrealistic.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, all the information I received from the Military Intelligence Service were forwarded to the main staff. Also, all knowledge that I had, operational and any other, were addressed to the main staff. But you see, Mr. President, on this map I could only move around within the enclave. I was not able to go to Zenica and to ask the commander of the 3rd Corps, "What are you doing? On the one hand we have a truce and on the other hand we have regrouping and preparations for an offensive." But I did ask my deputy, Nakic, to propose a meeting at which we would discuss the agreements reached and the implementation of those agreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You must admit that it is rather complicated to see what your role was in all this. I give the floor to Judge Rodrigues. From time to time we have to ask some clarification, because a dry chronology of events like this is difficult to understand, I must admit, especially for somebody who is not a military man like me, except when there's a war we know more or less who is waging war against who. Judge Rodrigues, do you have a better understanding than me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I am not a military man, but I have some questions though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I have a doubt that has been bothering me for several days. The Croats of Bosnia, the Muslims of Bosnia, were a whole. They were co-operating. They had joint commissions, joint meetings, et cetera, and all this to fight the enemy which were the Serbs. If we look at this relief, I think that the Serbs could see, observe, watch the fighting between the Croats and the Muslims. Why didn't the Serbs come in and resolve this problem? If we look at the maps, we see that the Serbs were everywhere. As I said, they could have watched you fighting. The relief itself tells us this. You're a military man, I'm not. Why did the Serbs not descend upon you and say, "Look, we have a solution for this problem." Why didn't they do that? Because, after all, that is the question to put. One has the impression that you were waging a war, but reality was quite different. It seems to me as if you were waging war in offices, meetings, agreements on a cease-fire. You reach an agreement today, tomorrow it's worth nothing, et cetera, et cetera. As you see, I have only just come and there are some things I don't understand and this is one of them. Who was, in fact, the enemy? And if there was a common enemy, why that common enemy did not take advantage of the opportunity to resolve the question definitely. Do you understand my question? You're a military man. If you had been on the other side, it would have been very easy if you see your enemy divided and fighting amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I shall try to answer this question. You are right as far as the situation as a whole is concern. It was indeed chaotic. I'll try to answer first your question why the Serbs didn't do something. Our front lines were very linked up with respect to the Serbs. When I say "we," I mean the HVO and the BH army in Travnik. Ever since the month of November 1992, and regardless of the fact that as a result of those conflicts we got this enclave, the front line in Travnik is still the same. About 80 kilometres of the front towards the Serbs is being held by the HVO and the rest by the BH army. Your question was: Why didn't the Serbs intervene and deal with the situation? Partly because of this fact that there was this long front line towards the Serbs. Another possibility or reality of the Serbs was that they also had, of their own priority, objectives at some other fronts. This is the month of March or April. At that time, the Serbs were fighting for their own strategic interests, and I assume that was not to gain control of Central Bosnia but to resolve their problems at the corridor, the Posavina corridor, to widen it, to deal with the problems in Eastern Bosnia, to link the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps with Eastern Bosnia, and so on. So I assume they also had their own priorities. I am describing this situation which I understand is difficult to comprehend, even for me as a military man. We had an agreement signed on the 21st of March, 1993, on the separation of forces. At the end of March, we had an agreement signed on a supreme joint command, but we had not managed to resolve this problem. I'm still functioning here. This is all manoeuvring area that I had. I couldn't reach Kiseljak or other areas, so all that was left for me to do was to avail myself of all possibilities, to have a meeting with the 3rd Corps commander and to insist on him on the implementation of the signed agreement so that we could focus on the front line with the Serbs. The joint command, at the level of the 3rd Corps and the Operative Zone, it had planned operations to liberate Vlasic. It had worked on plans, on maps. On the other hand, we had this influx of refugees and some other highly chaotic situations. I don't know whether I have made myself clear in my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, General. I think you have helped me to get a better understanding of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, would you agree that what the Judges are saying is true, that this was an absurd situation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was an absurd situation. That is what I do believe, but I'm speaking about what actually happened and what the reality was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us just go a little forward in the chronology. When did the joint commission of the 3rd Corps and the Operative Zone cease to operate? Could you explain that to the Court and then maybe the whole situation will become a little clearer.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The joint command at the level of the 3rd Corps and the Operative Zone ceased to operate when the BH army captured Travnik, the town of Travnik. That was on the 6th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let me avoid any leading questions. In fact, how many enemies did the BH army have in the spring of 1993? Actual fact, which armies was it fighting in 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And who was the HVO fighting in 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: With the BH army and the army of Republika Srpska. But we have another situation, if Their Honours would allow me to explain, the situation in Bihac, where the Bosniak Muslims are fighting with the Serbs against the Bosniak Muslims and the Croats within the Bihac pocket. That too was the reality in those days. The Bihac pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So, in fact, Croats and Muslims were fighting together against Muslims and Serbs in the Bihac pocket. You're referring to the followers of Alija Izetbegovic and the followers of Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The forces of the 5th Corps of the BH army and the HVO of Bihac were fighting together against the Muslim followers of Fikret Abdic and the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And is it true that Fikret Abdic was the Vice-President, the deputy of Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he won the greatest number of votes at the elections as a member of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but he ceded his position to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, so he became president.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us consider a hypothesis. Had the Serbs from Vlasic launched a decisive offensive down these hills and entered the Lasva River Valley, what do you think? Would the conflict between the BH army and the HVO have ceased or would there have been a joint resistance?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Didn't it suit the Serbs' interests just to watch and wait, to watch their enemies fighting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Of course, that suited their interests, and, in fact, from Vlasic they contributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: By shelling with the artillery sometimes Zenica and sometimes Vitez. In the course of '93, Colonel Stewart came to see me to ask for information as to whether the UNPROFOR base was within the range of the Serb artillery, and I told him "The shell that did not explode in Nova Bila is there, so you can check for yourself and see that we are within the range."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But let us return from the strategic global issues to the specific situation on the 21st of May, 1993. Again, you had a contact with the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received a report from the assistant for security that some other things needed to be done for the report on Ahmici to be completed. I asked him then to submit to me what he had managed to collect until then, that is, the 21st of May, '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us go on to the next day then.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The next day was the 22nd of May, 1993, and I again asked Mr. Franjo Nakic to raise the issue of the meeting with the commander of the 3rd Corps at the joint command meeting. Once again, I failed to reach the commander of the military police, and the local military police commander in Novi Travnik had formed his own checkpoint contrary to my orders and contrary to my position. Again, I received information from the security service that they were unable to complete the report, and again I insisted that they send me what they had collected so far pursuant to my order. I again received information that in each of the municipalities under HVO control in the Lasva River Valley, there were about 100 criminals or, rather, various groups of criminals, who had divided up the territory, who were engaging in black marketeering, and for the sake of recognition, they had shaved off their hair. They were skinheads, in other words. On the 23rd of May, 1993, early in the morning, there was an all-out attack in the area of Krcevine and Jardol in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: By members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. This was an attempt to re-link Stari Vitez via Krcevine and Jardol to the Muslim-controlled areas of Bukve and Preocica. In the course of the day, I again asked that the military police go to Ovnak to replace the military policemen at the checkpoint there. Instead of an answer, in front of the Vitez Hotel, there was a large group of people cursing and insulting and later shooting bursts of fire into the air in front of the hotel in front of my offices and headquarters indicating what they thought of my orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, why did you want to remove the military policemen from the checkpoint at Ovnak?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to remove them from that checkpoint because they themselves belonged to these gangs in the Lasva Valley and from Zenica. The black market was flourishing via this checkpoint of all goods in short supply, cigarettes in the first place, alcohol, cars, and a series of other products.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: "Black market" is the term used for illicit trade?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the course of the day, I also asked that the trucks carrying humanitarian aid and gas to Zenica should be allowed to pass, and I was told that the special purpose unit of the BH army known as the Black Swans, Crni Labudovi, had set out from Igman towards Konjic and partly towards Fojnica. This was a special purpose unit under the command of the main staff of the BH army. On the 24th of May, '93, at the morning meeting, I told the assistant for security not to come to the meeting again until he brings with him a written report on the results of the investigation into Ahmici. After that, I received a delegation of the European Monitoring Mission who requested that I provide written guarantees for the free passage of the convoy from Tuzla to Split and back consisting of 250 trucks. At the meeting with officers of the European Monitoring Mission, I tried to explain to them that the corridor they wanted to use was not safe and that it wouldn't be advisable for the convoy to use that route, so I proposed that two safer routes be chosen: one going from Tuzla via Visoko and Kiseljak to Konjic and Mostar, and the other one, an alternative route, from Tuzla via Zenica, Busovaca, and Kiseljak to Konjic and Mostar. In spite of my warnings that the route through the Lasva River Valley and in this pocket was not safe and the fact that I didn't provide a written guarantee, they left the meeting, and we will see later on that the convoy did come through the corridor, through the Lasva Valley, though I had told them that the forces were confronted at 50 to 100 metres from the main road, that units were in contact there, and it was simply impossible to provide written guarantees for the safety of the convoy. I was also told by the Military Intelligence Service that combat readiness of all the forces of the 3rd Corps of the BH army had been raised to a higher level and that an all-out offensive against the HVO was probably imminent. At 10.00, I also had a meeting with the commanders at which we reviewed the current military situation and tried to organise ourselves for defence in the event of an all-out attack by the BH army. I asked the commanders at that meeting to go public with the names and surnames of all persons who were persecuting and evicting Bosniak Muslims from their homes in the territories under the control of the HVO. I also asked the commanders that if they were incapable of eliminating those criminals, that they at least provide me with a list of names. At 12.00 hours, I attended a meeting in the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade where I was informed that the balance of forces between the BH army and the Busovaca HVO was six-to-one in favour of the BH army and that the length of the front was between 35 and 40 kilometres in Busovaca. We also reviewed the possible axes of attack, Kuber-Kaonik and Kacuni-Prosje. I made it clear to the brigade command that I was familiar with the negative response to my order prohibiting eviction of Bosniak Muslims from their apartments in the town of Busovaca, but I re-emphasised that it was our duty to do everything in our power for civilians to be safe in their homes and that it was our duty to guarantee them that safety. I also requested at the meeting that all participants take a positive attitude toward all international institutions, that is, that they cooperate with them. On the 25th of May, 1993, I received information from the assistant for security on the results of the investigation in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps we can go on to that document. I thought we should deal with Stari Vitez first. But, anyway, it is document D342, 3-4-2. Could a copy be given to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am going to read the document. It is the Security and Information Service, the forward command post of Vitez, "in the hands of the Commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic," the date is the 25th of May, 1993, the number is 82/93. The subject is "Information submitted." "As file enclosure, we submit to you information about the events in the village of Ahmici, Vitez Municipality. "This information encompasses operative findings and eyewitness accounts of these events, as well as an on-the-spot review of the site. The information is not complete and the case has not been definitively resolved, because in these areas combat activities continue to take place and it was not possible to obtain written statements from more key eyewitnesses. "Moreover, statements were not obtained from persons of Muslim nationality who, after the events in the village of Ahmici, fled to the Municipality of Zenica, to Travnik and elsewhere. In this respect, adequate collaboration by the opposite side was also lacking for the completion of this case. "After the cessation of combat activities and the creation of more favourable conditions, all necessary measures and actions will be taken in order to shed light upon this case completely." The signature is the aide to the commander for the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Vitez, Anto Sliskovic, and it says "Enclosure, 1." Tell us, please, General, do I understand this correctly, that along with this document, there was another report on the results of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, along with this document, as Enclosure 1, was a report on the results of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, what that report contained, the report that we don't have here?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to recall the report and to retell it, but I do know that there were some vague intimations in it and that it was not a precise report with regard to the perpetrators of the crime, which is what I had requested, and with regard to the circumstances in which the victims lost their lives, and it offered, for the most part, alternative information in the sense of the fact that it was possible that one group of people had done it and perhaps somebody else, so it was not a precise report nor was it a complete report, and it is difficult to give you the gist of the report now because I really don't recall all the details of it at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did it contain the names of the perpetrators of the crime?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, it did not contain concrete names of the perpetrators of the crime, but it is possible that it did speak about one or two or three names. That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the military police was mentioned or not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, it did not mention the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You say that the report, to the best of your recollection, gave some alternatives as to who the perpetrators could have been. Do you recall who was encompassed within these alternative possibilities? Who was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, groups were mentioned, but I'm saying this only on the basis of recollection. In black, then there was mention of the members of HOS, there was also mention of some groups that had been infiltrated, but there were no concrete names or surnames.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you understand this report to be a provisional report, that is to say, that the investigation was carried on, or as a definite report by the service sent to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I understood this exclusively as a provisional report, and I emphasised to the assistant forces that I insist upon having names and surnames, and from the report it can be seen, particularly in the latter part, and it concludes that the investigation will be continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, this complete report, did it go towards the superiors? Was it sent to the superiors in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it went to the main staff and to the security service. All the information was sent to the security service in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It was translated "this complete report." I asked about this particular report, the document we have, D342, and the report that was attached to this document. Was it sent to the superior authorities?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, who it was sent to and who sent out the report?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I sent one copy to the main staff of the HVO and the assistant for security sent one to the head -- department for security which was in Mostar, the Defence Ministry in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, on that day, the 25th of May, you also had a meeting of the Vitez government. They invited you, for the first time, to attend a meeting of the Vitez government. What did the civilian authorities of the Vitez government want of you? What was the meeting devoted to?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the first time that I was invited to attend a meeting of the municipal government, the civilian government of Vitez, and along with the minutes there was discussion of the problem of Stari Vitez. The civilian authorities stressed the daily casualties of civilians and the citizens of Vitez who suffered from the snipers of the BH army coming from Stari Vitez. They raised two issues, for the most part. One issue was that the forces of the BH army and HVO be separated, with the help of UNPROFOR, and to enable all the soldiers who had been brought in from outside, into Stari Vitez under the supervision of the BH army should leave Stari Vitez, and that this entire area be demilitarised and that the snipers be withdrawn. The second issue that was raised was to give an ultimatum of 48 hours, a 48-hour ultimatum, and then attack Stari Vitez, and to undertake all security measures and protection for the citizens and civilians from Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you accept the idea to organise an attack against Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I was resolutely against that, and I told the representatives of the Vitez government that it was impossible to launch an attack on Stari Vitez, along with issuing guarantees for the security and safety of the citizens because the civilians and the soldiers were located on the same premises, in the same features, and that every house was practically a military facility and a facility where Bosniak Muslims lived in Stari Vitez, although at the time Vitez had very many casualties from snipers, the BH army. I was resolutely against the second solution of any type of attack and combat operations against Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What were you afraid of if the HVO soldiers were to enter Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, quite certainly there would be heavy casualties which would be unavoidable in military operations of this type, because an attack on an inhabited area is always the most complicated military action to perform for everyone, and it is always difficult to control the situation under such circumstances. Quite certainly, there would be a great deal of civilian casualties and people would suffer, those people that lived in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you, on that occasion or ever afterwards, ever order a general all-out attack on Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The internal front within your enclave around Stari Vitez, did that represent a problem for you in view of the engagement and deployment of forces?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: That was a great problem, and not only with regard to the engagement of forces but also with regard to the very intense activity of snipers from the positions which overlooked the life of the town, and there were daily civilian casualties and others in the town of Vitez itself, that is to say, civilians who lived under the area controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: For a moment, in order to clarify matters, let us leave behind the supposed civilian casualties. In view of the size of Stari Vitez, the number of soldiers that defended it, were you able to take control of it, militarily speaking, if we were to forget for a moment the civilian casualties that this would incur?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, we could have had a military take-over. There would not be difficulties there because Stari Vitez is an enclave within an enclave, but I never even gave it a thought because it would be impossible to avoid having civilian casualties and great destruction. Were there no civilians there and only soldiers, then, of course, we could have taken control of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you please remind the Court how big the enclave was, approximately speaking?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a maximum of 1.500, 800 metres. I don't know whether it was that big.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a slight problem. Our client has an eye infection and this is causing him a great deal of difficulty and giving rise to headaches. So may we go on for another 15 or 20 minutes and then finish for the day? We will try to see that he gets medical help tomorrow. This has been going on for several days now and the eye condition has not improved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think my colleagues agree. Very well. We will continue for as long as you wish. Shall we have a ten-minute break first or shall we go on working for 15, 20 minutes? What do you prefer, General Blaskic? Would you like us to have a ten-minute break for you to rest and then continue for a quarter of an hour, or would you prefer us to stop at quarter past five or ten past five without a break in the meantime? Have you understood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may speak on behalf of my client. I'm trying to find out whether the doctor is in tomorrow morning at the prison, and if so, whether possible General Blaskic could see him at 10.00, if we didn't start until 11.00 or 11.30. If we can take a ten-minute break, I can call them once again. I've been calling this afternoon, and they haven't been able to tell me yet whether the doctor is in tomorrow at all. If we can take a break, I could call, and then if any adjustment in the schedule is necessary, we'll know what's needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me make a suggestion then. Mr. Hayman, I suggest that we have a ten-minute break. We will resume at 5.00, unless you haven't finished your telephone conversation you will tell Mr. Dubuisson, and if that is all right then we will continue for 15, 20 minutes. Tomorrow we will not begin before 10.30; isn't that right, Mr. Dubuisson? So that is how we're going to proceed. Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Gentlemen, it may be convenient if I said to you on the resumption either today or tomorrow, I may be referring to the transcript, so you may wish to arm yourself with the material. It's the transcript of the 15th of February, 1999, afternoon, at page 17625 and 17650. It shows that Mr. Hayman was right, though with a possible qualification which I want to propose when we discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, dear colleague. Very well, we're going to have a ten-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Mr. Hayman, were you able to have this telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. There will be a nurse available early tomorrow morning, so General Blaskic can be here at 10.30 as scheduled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. General Blaskic, you can now testify 15 minutes more, more or less? Can you hear me? My question was: Can you testify for, let's say, 15 minutes? We can stop at half past five. Is it okay? Yes?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now I could hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well, General. We left off at 25th of May, 1993. Could you please continue?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In the afternoon hours of 25 May, 1993, I had a meeting with the chief of civilian police in the town of Vitez, Mr. Mirko Samija, and we mostly discussed the issues of public law and order, and issues of the overall security in Vitez. Mr. Samija, chief of the civilian police, also raised the issue of the sniper activities, focusing on three positions, that is, that of Stari Vitez, Grbavica and Sljibcica. These were snipers of the BH army. He also pointed out the problem of shelling in the centre of Vitez itself and the problem of criminal gangs in the municipality. The chief of the civilian police told me that these criminal gangs were so strong that he does not have enough manpower to engage in a radical confrontation with these criminal gangs. The next day, on 26 May, now, 1993, I was again informed by the chief of staff, Mr. Franjo Nakic, about the plans for preparation of joint plans of the joint command of the HVO and the BH army concerning the liberation of Mount Vlasic, and about the fact that Nakic and General Merdan visited the HVO positions at Kula and positions of the BH army in Pezici. Nakic gave me his impressions that there was a serious lack of discipline there, and he said, literally, that people were unruly and that they were very tense on both sides. He mentioned that it was the case with both the BH army and the HVO soldiers. Also on the 26th of May, I conducted an investigation of why the UNHCR delegation did not visit this village of Krcevine and who prevented this visit from taking place. I received information that word had come from the Vitez Brigade that the road going to Krcevine was under the control of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and what I mean by "control" is firing control, and that they had warned the representatives of UNHCR regarding this portion of the road but that physically they did not prevent these representatives from taking this road. I also was informed that the BH army forces were again regrouping in Travnik and in the town of Travnik the tensions were running high between the HVO and the BH army. On that day I also received information from the Vitez Brigade commander, who confirmed to me that the BH army had taken the Saracevica feature at Mount Kuber as early as 15 April, 1993. At 11.00, I met with Colonel Duncan and we discussed several issues. The first issue was the military situation in the Lasva pocket, then the logistics problems, and lack of food stocks and general supplies, further security matters, and the existence of armed gangs in the territory of the Lasva Valley. I especially pointed out that we did not have an interest in having a conflict with the BH army or a war, and I again asked Colonel Duncan to exert additional pressure on the 3rd Corps commander so that a meeting between myself and the 3rd Corps commander would be organised. I told Colonel Duncan that, unfortunately, we are most fiercely attacked by the victims of persecution, and he asked me what I meant by that. I said that in the operative group of Bosnian Krajina of the BH army in Travnik, that it mostly consisted of people who had been expelled from the Bosnian Krajina and that they were members of the 1, 7, and 27th Bosnian Krajina Brigade, and were now placed in a position to fight for their space at the cost of Croats. I also was looking into the possibility to find some solutions for the refugees who were streaming into Travnik on a daily basis; in other words, to find some collective accommodations for them rather than keep them in the barracks because they were absorbed into the armed forces that way which further tipped the balance of power in favour of the BH army. On the 27th of May, 1993, I was informed by the security service that a meeting had been arranged between the representatives of the security office of the 3rd Corps and the security office of the Operative Zone, and it was regarding organising a joint convoy for supplies which would go both to the BH army and the HVO in Central Bosnia. I also asked for an investigation and some measures for those who had thrown Nasim Ahmic out of his apartment, and I think that he was from Vitez. On that day, information also came that Commander Stjepan Tuka from Fojnica had still not been relieved of his duty. The Military Intelligence Service informed me that the BH army was bringing in fresh troops to Grbavica from the village of Bukve and that they were digging in in the village and fortifying themselves in the village of Bukve and it consisted of digging foxholes and trenches and dugouts connecting them. The command post at Grbavica was in Pescara which was across from the UN base, and according to the military intelligence sources, the objective was to connect Stari Vitez with Divjak. During the day, I also received information that in Vitez, a Muslim family was thrown out of their apartment, and I asked that the necessary measures be taken and that the family be returned to their apartment, and I also received information that Miro Kozic and Srecko Maresovic were the ones who were involved in this illegal expulsion. On the 28th of May, 1993, officers from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Wait for a second. General, do I understand that on the 16th of May, when you meet Colonel Duncan, you do not talk at all about Ahmici, although you mentioned Ahmici when you met him on the 9th of May, 1993. In between you received the report, and if I understood well, the incident of Ahmici was not referred to. You do not mention the investigation, you do not say to him, "I've done my job." Nothing is said about Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In the meeting of the 26th of May, we did not talk about this, Mr. President, not during -- not in the meeting of the 26th of May. My interpretation said that you were asking about the 16th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: There was some confusion over the interpretation. I believe that your question was regarding the 26th of May, which is exactly what Mr. Blaskic had mentioned, but somehow "16th of May" was heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I will rephrase my question which is just, in fact, a confirmation. If I understood you well, on the 26th of May, at 11.00, you met Colonel Duncan. You talk about the military situation, about various hardships, you talk about security issues and groups of armed men. However, you do not mention the problem of Ahmici which, however, you mentioned and you talked about at length during the 9th of May meeting. So you didn't mention this issue during the meeting of the 26th of May, did you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in my notes, I do not have this -- I don't have that this issue was raised, it's just not in my notes, so my belief is that we did not discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am not questioning your notes, General Blaskic, and I'm following your testimony. That's why I'm asking this question. I will remind you that since the day before, you've had a report, however vague, but still you have the report which was your contribution, or the contribution of your command, to the investigation so as to find who was responsible for the massacre in Ahmici, and my question was: Nobody mentioned Ahmici that day. The commander of UNPROFOR didn't and you didn't either.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I have noted that we had talked about the gangs, but I do not have any notation with respect to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a convenient time, gentlemen, to take the witness back to the 9th of May when you had this conversation with Colonel Duncan. During that conversation, were you asked how matters might have developed at Ahmici and did you give three possibilities to which I referred earlier today: (a) that the crimes might have been perpetrated by the Serbs; (b) they might have been perpetrated by Muslims -- I think I said "Mujahedeen" this morning, but the transcript says Muslims; and (c) that they might have been perpetrated by Muslims masquerading in HVO uniforms. Did you give either of those three possibilities on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: What I had mentioned in the meeting of 9 May and which I have in my notes is that it was possible that these were men in black uniforms, and when Colonel Duncan asked clarification as to who was wearing black uniforms, I told him that it was the members of HOS, H-O-S, who did so. I know that I don't have a note nor did I ever contemplate that it was the Serbs who committed the crime nor do I have any notation about potentially Muslims who were disguised in uniforms were the perpetrators of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So if evidence was given in this court that you offered these three possible explanations, you say that evidence would not be correct, that you didn't offer those three possible explanations?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: What I said is what I had taken down in the way of notes in my logbook, and that is not what I had offered as explanations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Thank you, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did Colonel Duncan discuss this subject with other people in the Lasva Valley at that time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I believe that he did because the practice was that commanders of the BritBat met with other officials, with mayors and military commanders and the representatives of civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, on the 26th of May, when you again spoke to Colonel Duncan, did you receive an approval from the main staff to offer the results of the provisional investigation to Colonel Duncan?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At that time, had the report which you had received regarding Ahmici been sent to the main staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not only was it already sent but it was also the SIS -- it was sent to SIS because it was always done on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is 5.30. Maybe it is a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the Judges of this Trial Chamber will start at 9.00 tomorrow morning in another case, and then we will resume the evidence of the witness at 10.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.38 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of March, 1999, at 10.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
